lede: A pulse sent out and caught again tells you how far away something is. Ships find the seabed that way, hospitals find a baby, engineers find cracks inside steel. There is one number in it that has to be handled carefully.
can: Explain why a measured echo time covers twice the distance you want
Turn an echo time into a distance, and a known distance into a speed
Say what ultrasound is, and what sonar and radar each send out

md: Shout at a cliff and a moment later the cliff shouts back. A ship finds the seabed the same way, and a hospital scanner finds a baby. Each of them sends a pulse out, waits, and times what comes back.

md:
A pulse that comes back has been on **two journeys**: out to whatever reflected it, and back again. The timer starts when the pulse leaves and stops when the echo arrives, so the time you are given always covers **both**.
That is the whole idea of this topic. Speed × time gives the **total** distance the pulse covered, and the distance you actually want is **half** of it.

prompt: A ship sends a sonar pulse straight down and times the echo. In the time its timer measures, how far does the pulse travel?
options: down to the seabed and back up again
across the surface to the seabed
answer: down to the seabed and back up again
explain: Both journeys — which is why the total has to be halved before it becomes a depth.

title: The echo rule, and its two directions
md:
**distance to the reflector = (speed × time) ÷ 2**
Going the other way, from a known distance to a speed: **speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time**. Whichever direction you work in, the factor of two appears exactly once, and neither form is printed anywhere in the paper.

A ship's sonar pulse returns 0.12 s after it was sent. Sound travels through sea water at 1500 m/s.
**Step 1** — total distance $= 1500 \times 0.12 = 180$ m.
**Step 2** — that covers down **and** back, so halve it.
**Step 3** — depth $= 180 \div 2 = 90$ m.
The depth must always come out smaller than the total, never larger.

prompt: A shout echoes back from a cliff 0.5 s later, and sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far away is the cliff, in m?
explain: $(340 \times 0.5) \div 2 = 85$ m. The sound covered 170 m altogether, and the cliff is half that away.

title: Why the journey is halved
md: The pulse travels out to whatever reflects it and back again, so the time you measure covers the depth twice. Halving is what turns a there-and-back measurement into a one-way distance, and a question that hands you the distance instead turns that factor of two the other way round.

prompt: The sonographer puts two markers on the screen and the machine prints a length in millimetres. Explain how a machine that only measures times can print a length, and say what else it has to be told before it can.

md:
**Ultrasound** is sound with a frequency greater than **20 000 Hz** — too high for a human ear, but still sound, so still **longitudinal** and still needing particles to travel through.
The specification gives it exactly two uses. In **medicine**, measuring the **head diameter of a foetus**. In **industry**, **detecting defects in metals**.

prompt: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency greater than ______ Hz.
explain: 20 000 Hz. The number is what earns the mark; 'very high-pitched' does not.

md:
Inside a steel casting the same rule does the work. A pulse sent in from the surface reflects at **every boundary** it meets: first from a crack, later from the far face. An engineer reads the **arrival times** and turns each one into a depth with the same halving.
An **earlier echo means a shorter distance**, which is how a flaw nobody can see is found and measured.

prompt: Two echoes come back from one pulse sent into a steel block. What does the earlier one tell the engineer?
options: something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface
the block is made of two different metals
the pulse is travelling faster near the surface
answer: something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface
explain: Earlier means nearer. The speed is the same throughout the block, so a shorter time can only mean a shorter journey.

text: 5. Sonar, radar, and the other direction

md:
Two systems, one principle, different waves. **Sonar** sends **pulses of sound** through water, to find the seabed, shoals of fish or wrecks. **Radar** sends **electromagnetic waves** through air, to find **aircraft and ships**.
And the factor of two runs backwards too: given a known distance and a there-and-back time, **double the distance first**, then divide by the time to get a speed.

title: GCSE Physics Revision "Ultrasound"
why: Four minutes on what ultrasound is and how a pulse-echo measurement turns a time into a distance.

prompt: A clap echoes back from a wall 34 m away, 0.2 s later. What is the speed of sound, in m/s?
explain: The sound covered $2 \times 34 = 68$ m in 0.2 s, so the speed is $68 \div 0.2 = 340$ m/s.

Echo questions are worth three or four marks and follow one shape: the rule, the substitution, the halving, the answer with its unit. Putting the halving inside the equation line protects three marks at once. A question that gives you a distance and asks for a speed turns that factor of two round.
